title: Research
section: Interdicting selfish routing under congestion and uncertainty
text:
Interdicting selfish routing under congestion and uncertainty


Main PhD project with Manish Bansal. Manuscript in preparation.


If an adversary can slow down a few links in a network, and the people using it re-route selfishly, which links should they hit? And how do you protect against it when you don’t know the demand?

Think of a road network, a data network, or a fleet of AI agents sharing infrastructure. An interdictor with a budget penalizes some links. The users then route selfishly in a congestion game until no one can improve alone. Because a congestion game can have several equilibria, I take the pessimistic view: when ties occur, the equilibrium is the one least favorable to the interdictor. That makes this a three-level max–min–min problem, and since the users’ problem is an integer program, the usual duality or KKT reformulations don’t apply.
What I built:

Two exact algorithms, with proofs that the bounds are valid and that they terminate: a column-and-constraint generation method that represents generated equilibria with indicator constraints, and a cutting-plane method with congestion-lifted optimality cuts, integer L-shaped cuts, and neighborhood cuts.
A distributionally robust version over a Wasserstein ambiguity set, with both algorithms extended scenario by scenario and an LP separation step.
A Python/Gurobi implementation tested in about 6,000 solver runs on a Slurm cluster.

NoteShow the formulation (sketch)





Interdiction \(x \in X\) (budgeted), user strategies \(y \in Y\), arc loads \(\ell_a(y)\), arc cost \(c_a(\ell, x_a)\) increasing in load and in interdiction:
\[
\max_{x \in X}\; \min_{y \in \mathcal{E}(x)} \; \sum_{a} \ell_a(y)\, c_a\big(\ell_a(y), x_a\big),
\qquad
\mathcal{E}(x) = \arg\min_{y \in Y} \; \sum_{a} \sum_{j=1}^{\ell_a(y)} c_a(j, x_a).
\]
The inner set \(\mathcal{E}(x)\) is the set of pure Nash equilibria, characterized as minimizers of the Rosenthal potential. The middle “min” is the pessimistic selection. See the manuscript for the exact model.

title: Research
section: Risk-averse scheduling for a data-center microgrid
text:
Risk-averse scheduling for a data-center microgrid


With Virginia Tech Electrical & Computer Engineering. Ongoing.


A data center’s power demand and its renewable supply are both uncertain. How do you schedule generators so that the worst days don’t cause blackouts, without overspending on the average day?


Reformulated microgrid unit commitment and economic dispatch as a two-stage risk-averse stochastic MILP, using CVaR to control Expected Energy Not Served in the tail scenarios.
Designed and implemented Benders decomposition for it in Python/Gurobi; currently scaling to full data-center instances.
Related: a deterministic MILP for operating a water distribution system (tank net-contribution model), built as the base for a distributionally robust extension.

title: Research
section: Pricing a product on the verge of withdrawal
text:
Pricing a product on the verge of withdrawal


With Anand Jacob Abraham (IIT Kharagpur). Submitted to Production Planning & Control, November 2026.


A manufacturer sells an end-of-life product through two competing retailers, and one of them may lose demand without warning. What wholesale price should the manufacturer commit to, and when does a retailer walk away?


Modeled it as a two-period Stackelberg game with asymmetric probabilistic demand disruption and a committed wholesale price.
Derived closed-form subgame-perfect equilibria in an interior regime and a KKT-characterized corner regime, including the exact threshold at which the disrupted retailer exits the clearance market.
Proved how the wholesale price responds in each regime, an exact profit-gap identity, and a lower bound on the manufacturer’s profit.

title: Research
section: Making a tidal simulation actually run
text:
Making a tidal simulation actually run


Master’s thesis at NIT Calicut with Satyananda Panda, revisited in 2026. Manuscript in preparation.


My thesis modeled tides in the Gulf of Khambhat with shallow-water equations, but the solver couldn’t simulate more than a short window. Two years later I found out why and fixed it.


The original implicit finite-volume/WENO solver (MATLAB) ran Newton solves with an \(O(N^2)\) dense finite-difference Jacobian at every step, at time steps far below the CFL limit.
I redesigned it as an explicit WENO5 + SSP-RK3 scheme with linear cost per step, in Python. Multi-cycle simulations went from intractable to seconds.
